title: A sign, and a father
carry: water is the father; don't pour out his gift
tomorrow: the chili seedlings need ground. whose garden do they go in?

lines: MY BOOK SAYS. MY GURU SAYS.
cards: A hot afternoon in the strip of dirt behind Arjan's building.
Bebe has come over with a tray of chili seedlings for Arjan's mom, and she's watering the bed with the hose running full blast, telling stories, paying no attention to the puddle. Mrs.
Haddad walks out, says hello, and quietly turns the tap down. Bebe raises an eyebrow. Mrs.
Haddad smiles: my book says every living thing was made from water. Bebe, never one to lose a quote-off, answers: my Guru says water comes first. Simran sets down her phone.

teach.b: Underneath the quote-off is an old question: is water just a utility, or is it sacred? Bebe's line is from Guru Nanak, in Asa di Var on Ang 472.
In paraphrase: first, water is life, by which everything is made green. And the Japji's closing lines, on Ang 8, name water the father.
A father is someone who provides, someone you come from, someone whose gift you don't pour on the ground. So the Sikh answer is family: you don't waste your father's water. Mrs.
Haddad's line is from the Qur'an, surah twenty-one, verse thirty.

teach.h: QUR'AN: EVERY LIVING THING OF WATER.
teach.b: In paraphrase: God made every living thing of water, and asks, will they not then believe? Shared ground, and it's real: two grandmothers, two books, one thirst.
Both see water as the beginning of life, not something to take for granted. And one honest difference. In the Qur'an, water's life-giving power is a sign, pointing the reader toward the Creator.
In the Japji, water sits inside a family picture, a father, beside a Guru and a mother.

Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: in the Japji's picture, air, water and earth are Guru, father and mother, and day and night are the two nurses in whose lap the whole world plays. Bebe looks at the puddle.
Then she reaches over and turns the hose off completely. Mrs. Haddad offers her a cutting of mint.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji, which names water the father, in morning prayer, and some gurdwaras and Sikh families treat saving water and caring for rivers as seva.

games.q: what does “water is the father” mean?
o: a blessing said over water before it's drunk
water as the one who provides, a gift you don't waste
a title of the Guru who dug wells for the villages

games.q: two grandmothers, two books — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an speaks of every living thing being made of water
surah 21, verse 30, in paraphrase: God made every living thing of water.
Guru Nanak and the Qur'an frame water in exactly the same way
shared ground, water as the beginning of life; but the Qur'an calls it a sign, and the Japji calls it a father.
calling water 'the father' is about respect, not just poetry
a father provides and you come from him; you don't waste his gift.

games.q: your roommate runs the shower for ten minutes before stepping in, 'to get it perfect.' going by today, what fits best?
o: mention, kindly, that water's a gift; maybe a bucket for the plants?
nothing; water bills are split, so it's not really your business.
turn the water heater down so the problem fixes itself.
games.why: water is the father: a gift you don't pour on the ground. said kindly, the way Mrs. Haddad turned the tap down.

practice: Fill a glass slowly from a tap, or pour water from one cup into another, and listen to it the whole time. When it's full, stop, and drink a little slowly. Whatever you don't drink, give to a plant instead of the sink.

wordCard.voice: Water is the father. From the Japji's last lines: water as the one who provides, whose gift you don't waste, because everything green begins with it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: paani, water. Paani pitaa: water the father (Ang 8).

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: water is the father; don't pour out his gift. Two grandmothers, one hose, day 1735.

Ang 8, Japji, closing salok ('pavan guru paani pitaa maataa dharat mahat'), paraphrased
Qur'an 21:30 (every living thing made of water), paraphrased
